bridges.description: Multiple independent lines of evidence jointly make theism more plausible than atheism.
A beginning and life-permitting order point to a transcendent personal creator and designer.
Objective moral values and duties require a divine personal foundation.
Resurrection evidence and personal experience identify and disclose God.
Christian purposes, freedom, and eternal life make evil compatible with God.
Apparently uncompensated suffering makes a morally perfect omnipotent and omniscient God extremely unlikely.
Arguments for a creator or supernatural cause do not establish the morally perfect God at issue.
Inductive logic carries known wrong-making features toward conclusions about total moral status.
Objective moral properties can be grounded without divine commands.
Religious experience, scripture, and resurrection claims do not identify a perfectly good God.

sections.title: Creator, Origin, and Design
sections.rationale: Cosmic beginning, fine-tuning, causal scope, and the attributes established by a creator inference form the debate's combined creator-evidence route.

sections.title: Inductive Probability and Property Reasoning
sections.rationale: The competing probability frameworks and the treatment of known and unknown moral properties govern the debate's central inductive inferences.

sections.title: Moral Reality and Grounding
sections.rationale: Both speakers treat the basis of objective moral facts and duties as central to the motion.

sections.title: Evil, Providence, and Perfection
sections.rationale: The main atheistic case and the principal theistic replies concern whether suffering fits a morally perfect God.

sections.title: Resurrection and Miracle Evidence
sections.rationale: The historical case turns on both the proposed resurrection explanation and the empirical prior plausibility of miracles.

sections.title: Religious Experience and Revelation
sections.rationale: Experiential warrant and the moral content attributed to scripture and Jesus bear on whether revelation discloses a perfect God.

sections.title: Divine Concept and Modal Coherence
sections.rationale: The competing definitions of God and coherence of necessary existence, goodness, foreknowledge, and freedom determine what counts as the God at issue.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The universe began to exist and therefore has a transcendent personal cause.
moves.warrant: An actual infinite past cannot exist, Big Bang cosmology supports an absolute beginning, and whatever begins to exist has a cause.
moves.inference: A cause of space and time must be timeless, spaceless, immaterial, powerful, and personal rather than an abstract object.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete first opening argument, from the finite-past case through the personal-cause conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Whatever begins to exist has a Cause
the cause of the universe is a Transcendent personal unembodied mind
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Craig opening after his announced restart and before his numbered second argument.
moves.importanceRationale: This is a principal independent route from the motion to a creator.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues directly for a personal creator from cosmic beginning.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is best explained by design.
moves.warrant: The constants and initial quantities occupy an extraordinarily narrow life-permitting range, are not fixed by physical law, and display an independently specified life pattern.
moves.inference: Physical necessity and chance are rejected, leaving design and therefore a cosmic designer.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete fine-tuning argument, including data, alternatives, pattern criterion, and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: physical necessity chance or design
therefore it is due to design
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous numbered argument in Craig's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: Fine-tuning is one of Craig's five main affirmative lines.

burdenContact.rationale: It infers an intelligent designer from life-permitting cosmic conditions.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Objective moral values and duties exist and require God.
moves.warrant: Naturalistic evolution can explain adaptive moral beliefs but not their objective truth, while moral experience presents acts such as cruelty and child abuse as genuinely wrong.
moves.inference: Because objective moral reality would not exist without God yet does exist, God exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This covers Craig's full moral syllogism, naturalistic contrast, experiential premise, and conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: rape cruelty and child abuse
some things at least are really wrong
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous third numbered argument in Craig's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the affirmative bridge from moral objectivity to God.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats God as the necessary foundation for objective morality.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The historical facts surrounding Jesus are best explained by resurrection and thereby support God's existence.
moves.warrant: Craig cites the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' otherwise unexpected resurrection belief as established facts without a plausible naturalistic explanation.
moves.inference: A divine resurrection would vindicate Jesus and entail God's existence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the full opening presentation of the three facts, rival-explanation claim, and theological conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are actually three established facts
there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation of these facts
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous fourth numbered argument in Craig's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Craig's main historical route to identifying God.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects resurrection evidence with God's existence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: God can be known directly through personal experience apart from argument.
moves.warrant: Biblical persons treated God as an experienced reality, and sincere seekers are promised direct awareness of God.
moves.inference: Immediate experience can rationally ground belief in God without external proofs.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span is Craig's complete fifth line, expressly framed as direct knowledge rather than an inferential proof.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments
simply by personally experiencing him
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous fifth numbered argument in Craig's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a distinct experiential basis for theism.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers direct religious experience as access to God.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: The debated God is an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect personal creator, and the evidential problem of evil makes such a being extremely unlikely.
moves.warrant: Tooley distinguishes his probabilistic thesis from a claim that evil and God are logically incompatible.
moves.inference: The con burden is to lower the probability of the defined God, not to prove logical impossibility or deny every supernatural cause.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This opening passage fixes Tooley's God concept and the exact probabilistic scope of his case.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God is by definition omnipotent
make it unlikely indeed extremely unlikely that God exists
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous beginning of Tooley's formally introduced opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the motion-level target and Tooley's adopted burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the evidential conclusion directed at the defined God.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: The world contains extensive suffering, divine hiddenness, and—conditionally on scripture—actions and institutions that appear gravely inconsistent with perfect goodness.
moves.warrant: Tooley catalogs moral, natural, animal, and bodily suffering, then explicitly treats hiddenness, scriptural violence, and hell as hypothetical evils conditional on an omnipotent being or the Testaments being true.
moves.inference: These cases supply the apparent evils to which the later probabilistic argument applies.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The full catalog and three expressly conditional categories are needed to preserve the argument's evidence base without converting suppositions into concessions.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: three kinds of what I call hypothetical evils
much less evident than it could be
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous catalog in Tooley's opening, with the conditional framing stated in the source.
moves.importanceRationale: The examples are the empirical inputs to Tooley's central argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the suffering and apparent divine actions whose probability is assessed.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Apparently unbalanced divine permission of disasters makes a morally perfect omnipotent and omniscient being unlikely.
moves.warrant: Known wrong-making features of permitting disasters lack known sufficiently weighty right-making features; if total wrongs remain unbalanced, such permission is wrong all things considered and incompatible with moral perfection.
moves.inference: The probabilistic step from known to total properties supports the conclusion that the defined God does not exist.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This contains the numbered argument and identifies its sole non-deductive transition.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: wrong making properties of the actions
morally wrong to do so all things considered
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous formal argument in Tooley's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Tooley's central motion-level argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It draws the atheistic conclusion from apparently unjustified suffering.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Inductive logic supports moving from known net wrongness to a probability greater than one-half of wrongness all things considered.
moves.warrant: For equally likely and equally weighty unknown right- and wrong-making properties, three of four possibilities leave the action wrong; Tooley generalizes this to many apparent evils.
moves.inference: As the number of apparent evils grows, the probability that none is wrong to permit becomes very low.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span preserves the intuitive four-case model, known/unknown distinction, generalization, and many-evil conclusion; shortening it would omit the offered warrant for the crucial induction.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: known right making wrong making properties
the probability that action a is morally wrong given all moral properties
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous technical explanation in Tooley's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the explicit warrant for the central probabilistic inference.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies Tooley's probability bridge from observed to total moral properties.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Suffering may serve the higher purpose of bringing persons freely to knowledge of God.
moves.warrant: Earthly happiness is not Christianity's primary purpose, and a world with natural and moral evils may yield the optimal number of freely formed relationships with God.
moves.inference: Tooley cannot infer gratuitousness without showing a feasible world with less suffering and equal salvific knowledge.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete first Christian-doctrine response and its explicit comparative-world burden.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the purpose of life is not happiness
another possible World which is feasible for God to create
moves.attributionRationale: First numbered response in Craig's announced rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests the claim that observed suffering lacks adequate purpose.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a divine purpose that could make evil compatible with God.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the inference from unknown compensating reasons to probable total wrongness by proposing a salvific purpose and feasible-world constraint.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Human moral evil is expected if humanity is in rebellion and alienation from God.
moves.warrant: Craig says people reject God's purpose, become morally guilty, and thereby display the depravity and need for forgiveness Christianity predicts.
moves.inference: The prevalence of moral evil is not surprising evidence against the Christian worldview.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete second numbered doctrine; it is separated from the afterlife reply because it explains moral agency rather than compensating suffering.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: mankind is in a state of rebellion against God
given his worldview he expects it
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous second numbered point in Craig's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies Craig's distinct explanation of human-caused evil.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes moral evil an expected result of free rebellion.

responseComponents.description: Explains the catalog's human moral evil through rebellion rather than divine moral defect.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Eternal life can outweigh even severe temporal suffering.
moves.warrant: Craig appeals to an afterlife of incomparable joy and argues that finite suffering shrinks toward an infinitesimal moment relative to eternity.
moves.inference: Temporal suffering need not make God's overall treatment wrong or improbable if eternal compensation is available.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete third numbered doctrine, separated because its warrant is eternal compensation rather than human rebellion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: knowledge of God flows over into eternal life
the sufferings of this life cannot even be compared
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous third numbered point and summary in Craig's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is an independent response to the weight of suffering.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers eternal compensation as a right-making context.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the all-things-considered wrongness inference by adding an eternal compensating good.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Tooley's greater-than-one-half premise rests on a controversial probability framework that does not yield objective real-world probabilities.
moves.warrant: Craig says the results depend on arbitrary theorist choices and that alternative approaches avoid those failings without supporting Tooley's premise.
moves.inference: If the probability rule is unsupported, the evidential-evil calculation loses its crucial inferential step.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's focused first critique of Tooley's probability basis.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: depends upon arbitrary decisions made by the theorist
these do not support his key premise
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous first numbered critique in Craig's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It targets the key warrant of Tooley's central argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It attacks the probability calculation used to infer incompatibility with goodness.

responseComponents.description: Denies that the proposed probability system supplies objective support for the known-to-unknown inference.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Whether permitting harm is wrong depends partly on the agent's authority, and God may have permissions humans lack.
moves.warrant: Craig contrasts a mother's authority over her child with a stranger's and argues that God, as giver of life, may end life where a human may not.
moves.inference: Tooley cannot transfer ordinary human prohibitions unchanged to divine action.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's first complete ground against Tooley's moral premise, isolated from his later metaethical and property-structure objections.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we always need to ask wrong for whom
God I think has the right to do or permit things that we don't
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous first numbered ground in Craig's premise critique.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests the moral standard applied to divine permission.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes moral permission sensitive to divine authority.

responseComponents.description: Challenges its premise that permitting the disaster is wrong for God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: A bad event does not by itself make permission wrongful, and an act's moral status cannot always be computed by summing isolated properties.
moves.warrant: The heart-surgeon example shows that context can transform what first appears to be a wrong-making feature rather than merely add an offsetting right-making feature.
moves.inference: Tooley's known-versus-unknown property arithmetic may misclassify divine permission before the relevant context is known.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This preserves Craig's distinct badness/wrongness distinction and heart-surgeon contextual argument as one coherent objection to additive property analysis.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Badness doesn't entail wrongness
it's a context in which we now see
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous third numbered objection in Craig's rebuttal; event 1361 introduces that objection.
moves.importanceRationale: It attacks the structural moral inference at the center of Tooley's evil argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies that observed badness fixes all-things-considered divine wrongness.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes a bad outcome from wrongful divine permission.
Challenges the additive treatment of right- and wrong-making properties.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: On Craig's divine-command view, God's permission is itself relevant to permissibility, so Tooley's contrary premise assumes the theory false.
moves.warrant: Craig defines wrongness through divine prohibition and notes that God did not forbid permitting the Haitian earthquake.
moves.inference: Using that permission as a premise against God begs the question against the offered moral theory.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's distinct fourth critique, separated because it alleges circularity within Tooley's argument rather than agent-relative authority or contextual holism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: an action is morally permissible if it is not forbidden by God
his argument turns out to be reasoning in a circle
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous fourth numbered critique in Craig's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies a separate alleged circularity in applying moral wrongness against God.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies Craig's divine-command foundation to the permission premise.

responseComponents.description: Argues that its moral premise presupposes rejection of divine-command ethics.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Hiddenness, scriptural violence, and hell do not independently defeat God's existence.
moves.warrant: Greater obviousness may not produce relationship; constant explanations could be counterproductive; Old Testament atrocities primarily challenge scriptural inerrancy; and hell results from free, persistent separation contrary to God's saving will.
moves.inference: Tooley's conditional revelation-based evils do not supply a clear atheistic inference.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact sequence answers Tooley's four expressly previewed hypothetical-evil categories in order.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: this is really an attack on biblical inherency
the only reason there's anybody in hell is due to human intransigence
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous closing portion of Craig's first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses revelation-linked extensions of the evil case.

burdenContact.rationale: It limits what scriptural and hiddenness claims establish about God.

responseComponents.description: Answers hiddenness, silence, Old Testament violence, and hell without treating Tooley's conditional assumptions as concessions.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Craig's cosmological and design arguments, even if sound, establish at most an intelligent immaterial cause rather than the morally perfect God Tooley defined.
moves.warrant: A fine-tuner could be perfectly good, indifferent, or evil, and Craig offers no premise preferring perfect goodness.
moves.inference: The creator conclusion does not by itself satisfy the motion-level divine attributes, so the arguments are incomplete as arguments for God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage identifies the shared gap across creator arguments and develops it with the fine-tuning case.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: not in fact Arguments for the existence of God
how can one possibly get from the above conclusion to the conclusion that God exists
moves.attributionRationale: Opening of Tooley's first rebuttal after the formal handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests the scope of Craig's central creator arguments.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates evidence for a designer from evidence for perfect goodness.

responseComponents.description: Argues that a personal cause lacks the full attributes of Tooley's defined God.
Argues that design does not select a perfectly good designer over indifferent or evil alternatives.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Craig's creator arguments do not make a perfectly good creator more probable than indifferent or evil alternatives.
moves.warrant: Tooley applies an equal a priori probability principle to incompatible moral-character properties, assigning symmetry among good, indifferent, and evil powerful designers.
moves.inference: Even taken together, the creator arguments cannot raise the probability of the perfectly good hypothesis above one-third.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the stated probability principle, its three-hypothesis application, and cumulative-case conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: have the same initial probability
none the probabilities can be greater than 1/3
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous probability application in Tooley's first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Tooley's formal probability reply to Craig's cumulative design case.

burdenContact.rationale: It uses probability symmetry to block identification of a good designer.

responseComponents.description: Claims fine-tuning evidence cannot privilege a good designer over morally indifferent or evil designers.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: A resurrection, even if granted, would show at most action by some supernatural being unless Craig links that agent to omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness.
moves.warrant: The historical conclusion does not itself identify the raising agent's full moral and modal attributes.
moves.inference: Without the missing identification premise, the resurrection case does not establish the defined God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Tooley's complete argument distinguishing a supernatural resurrection cause from God.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: raised from the dead by some supernatural being or other
no value at all as an argument for the existence of God
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous resurrection subsection in Tooley's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It attacks the key identity bridge in Craig's historical argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that resurrection evidence underdetermines the divine agent.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the step from a resurrection event to the defined God.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: A necessarily existing temporal person is an incoherent basis for moral necessity.
moves.warrant: Tooley argues that parallel ontological reasoning can generate incompatible necessarily existing beings—perfectly good, indifferent, and perfectly evil—and therefore cannot establish any of them.
moves.inference: Apart from timeless abstract objects, a necessarily existing entity in time is said to be self-contradictory, which later blocks God as the ground of necessary moral truths.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is the complete ontological parody and contradiction argument later invoked in Tooley's moral-grounding reply; retaining it prevents that later move from depending on an omitted target.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: one can also generate contradiction
no type of argument that generates contradictory conclusions can possibly be sound
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous ontological subsection in Tooley's first rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the modal premise used in the later necessary-moral-truth argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies that a necessarily existing personal God can uniquely ground necessary moral truth.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Religious experience does not reliably disclose objective divine reality.
moves.warrant: Experiences across religions support incompatible beliefs, and their content strongly correlates with prior religious formation.
moves.inference: Peer disagreement and belief-content correlation undercut the initial justification supplied by a private experience.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Tooley's two complete defeaters: incompatible experiences and prior-belief correlation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: experiences that equally justify initially religious beliefs
content of one's religious experiences are very strongly correlated
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous experience subsection in Tooley's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers Craig's distinct experiential route.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers defeaters for personal religious experience.

responseComponents.description: Argues that conflicting and culturally correlated experiences defeat their objective evidential force.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Craig has not shown that objective moral value is impossible without God.
moves.warrant: Many philosophers defend non-theological accounts of objective value, and refuting that possibility requires examining and defeating those accounts rather than citing an evolutionary error theory.
moves.inference: The first premise of Craig's moral argument remains unsupported.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Tooley's focused reply to the no-God/no-objective-value premise and its stated burden.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: non-theological accounts of the existence of objective values
William Lane Craig does not discuss any of these philosophers
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous moral-argument subsection in Tooley's rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It targets the main disputed premise in Craig's moral syllogism.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves live secular realist alternatives to divine grounding.

responseComponents.description: Denies that Craig has ruled out objective morality on atheism.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: A minimal but ordinary God concept is a supreme personal creator distinct from the world, and Craig's arguments cumulatively add power, moral foundation, and resurrection.
moves.warrant: The cosmological and design conclusions give an uncreated timeless personal creator and designer, while the other arguments supply further attributes and actions.
moves.inference: Rejecting the label God while granting the cumulative profile would be an unusually narrow form of atheism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete response to the definition gap, including the minimal concept and cumulative supplementation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a common sense minimal definition of God
they do constitute a powerful cumulative case
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous opening of Craig's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly defines Craig's adopted motion burden and cumulative method.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how separate arguments jointly reach Craig's conception of God.

responseComponents.description: Answers that a personal creator is an ordinary minimal God concept and gains further attributes cumulatively.
Rejects treating each argument as isolated from the other offered evidence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Complete ignorance about alternatives does not assign them equal precise probabilities.
moves.warrant: The marble-bag example shows that assigning one-half to red versus non-red conflicts with analogous assignments for other colors; an interval from zero to one better represents ignorance.
moves.inference: Tooley's equal-prior allocation among good, indifferent, and evil creators is arbitrary.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes Craig's symmetry-of-ignorance concession, full marble illustration, interval alternative, and application.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a sort of symmetry of ignorance about competing views
any precise assessment becomes quite arbitrary
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous probability reply in Craig's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests Tooley's probability basis for the designer alternatives.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends design inference against equal-prior dilution.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the move from lack of evidence to precise equal probabilities.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Secular moral realism affirms values and duties without adequately explaining their objective status or authority.
moves.warrant: Abstract values include vices as well as virtues and cannot issue obligations; naturalism supplies no personal authority for moral imperatives.
moves.inference: Absent an explanatory ground, evolutionary illusion is more plausible on naturalism, while objective evil supports God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This contains Craig's direct response to secular realist alternatives, including the distinct problem of obligation.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there's no good reason to think that those theories are true
there isn't any person or authority to issue such moral imperatives
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous moral-argument reply in Craig's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It defends the central premise of Craig's moral argument against Tooley's alternative accounts.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that objective value and duty need personal divine explanation.

responseComponents.description: Replies that secular realist accounts lack an explanation of moral status and obligation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The historical context identifies the raiser of Jesus as the God of Israel rather than an unspecified supernatural being.
moves.warrant: Jesus presented himself as the revelation of Israel's God and was executed for blasphemous claims; resurrection would publicly vindicate those claims.
moves.inference: The best explanation of the resurrection facts is action by the God Jesus proclaimed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Craig's complete identification bridge from resurrection to the God of Israel.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the supernatural being that raised Jesus from the dead was the god of Israel
publicly Vindicated Jesus of Nazareth
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous resurrection reply in Craig's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the missing identity premise challenged by Tooley.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects the alleged miracle to a specific divine agent.

responseComponents.description: Answers that Jesus' claims and execution context identify the raising agent as Israel's God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Religious experience can rationally justify belief unless a defeater is supplied.
moves.warrant: Craig does not deny Muslim experience can initially justify belief; he distinguishes initial warrant from later reasons against a religion.
moves.inference: Conflicting experiences alone do not defeat Christian experience, and Tooley has not supplied a successful Christian defeater.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span is Craig's complete defeater-based reply to religious disagreement.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I think a Muslim is Justified
absent in tonight's debate is any good defeaters
moves.attributionRationale: Closing portion of Craig's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves Craig's answer to the main objection against experiential warrant.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends experiential knowledge through a defeater condition.

responseComponents.description: Argues that disagreement does not automatically remove initial experiential justification.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Necessary basic moral truths cannot depend ontologically on a personal God.
moves.warrant: If God is not necessarily existent, moral truths still hold in possible worlds without God; if a temporally existing person is declared necessary, Tooley argues that supposition generates contradiction.
moves.inference: States of affairs involving God cannot be the sole truth-makers for basic moral truths.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This contains Tooley's full modal argument against divine grounding of necessary moral truths.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: basic moral truths are necessary truths
States Affairs involving God cannot provide an ontological ground for basic moral truths
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous first moral argument in Tooley's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It offers a positive modal objection to the divine-grounding premise.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that moral necessity extends beyond worlds containing God.

responseComponents.description: Rejects God's necessity as the condition for objective morality.
Offers modal truth across possible worlds as an alternative grounding constraint.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: A command-based account fails to make God's own infliction of suffering objectively wrong.
moves.warrant: If wrongness consists in God's commands to persons and God does not command himself, then the account leaves divine action outside the prohibition on inflicting suffering.
moves.inference: The proposed theory denies objective rights against God and cannot ground the moral premise Craig needs.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Tooley's complete second argument against the divine-command account, through its stated nihilism conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God does not command himself not perform any actions
persons and sentient beings do not have any objective intrinsic rights
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous second moral argument in Tooley's second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly tests Craig's moral foundation against divine conduct central to the evil debate.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges divine command theory as a basis of objective wrongness.

responseComponents.description: Argues that divine authority cannot erase objective wrongness toward sentient beings.
Argues that command-based wrongness improperly exempts God's own actions.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: If Yahweh raised Jesus, scriptural portrayals give reason to deny that the agent was perfectly good.
moves.warrant: Tooley cites the flood, death of Egyptian firstborn, commands against Amalekites, capital penalties, and eternal hell as attributed acts.
moves.inference: The historical-context identification of Yahweh does not bridge to the morally perfect God and may point away from that identification.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Tooley's full conditional resurrection-agent argument and the scriptural warrant offered for its key premise.
